Hands-on Exercise 10: Information Dashboard Design

  • Show All Code
  • Hide All Code
  • View Source
Author

Bao Sihan

1 Overview

This hands-on exercise is based on Chapter 31, which focuses on information dashboard design in R. In this page, I work on three main ideas: bullet charts, sparklines, and dashboard-style tables.

To make the file easier to render in my local environment, I use the prepared CoffeeChain.rds file saved in ../data/ instead of importing the original Access database.

The goals of this exercise are:

  • to build a bullet chart for product sales comparison,
  • to create sparkline views for monthly sales trends,
  • to combine charts and tables into compact dashboard-style outputs,
  • to create an interactive table with hover values in a stable way.

2 Getting started

2.1 Packages used

Show code 
required_pkgs <- c(
  "tidyverse", "lubridate", "ggthemes", "gt",
  "reactable", "htmltools", "scales"
)

optional_pkgs <- c("gtExtras")

missing_required <- required_pkgs[
  !vapply(required_pkgs, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)
]

missing_optional <- optional_pkgs[
  !vapply(optional_pkgs, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)
]

if (length(missing_required) > 0) {
  install.packages(missing_required, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
}

if (length(missing_optional) > 0) {
  try(
    install.packages(missing_optional, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org"),
    silent = TRUE
  )
}

invisible(lapply(required_pkgs, library, character.only = TRUE))

has_gtextras <- requireNamespace("gtExtras", quietly = TRUE)
if (has_gtextras) {
  library(gtExtras)
}

2.2 Importing the prepared data

Show code 
coffeechain <- readr::read_rds("../data/CoffeeChain.rds") %>%
  mutate(Date = as.Date(Date))

2.3 Preparing product-level totals

Show code 
product <- coffeechain %>%
  group_by(Product) %>%
  summarise(
    target = sum(`Budget Sales`, na.rm = TRUE),
    current = sum(Sales, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(Product = forcats::fct_reorder(Product, current))

2.4 Preparing the 2013 monthly report

Show code 
report_base <- coffeechain %>%
  mutate(Year = year(Date), Month = month(Date)) %>%
  filter(Year == 2013) %>%
  group_by(Product, Month) %>%
  summarise(
    Sales = sum(Sales, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Budget Sales` = sum(`Budget Sales`, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  tidyr::complete(
    Product,
    Month = 1:12,
    fill = list(Sales = 0, `Budget Sales` = 0)
  ) %>%
  arrange(Product, Month)

3 Bullet chart in ggplot2

The chart below recreates the product-level bullet chart idea from the chapter. The grey bars provide reference ranges, the black bar shows actual sales, and the red marker shows the target value.

Show code 
bullet_data <- product %>%
  mutate(
    range3 = pmax(target, current) * 1.05,
    range2 = target * 0.80,
    range1 = target * 0.50
  )

ggplot(bullet_data, aes(x = Product)) +
  geom_col(aes(y = range3), fill = "grey85", width = 0.82) +
  geom_col(aes(y = range2), fill = "grey70", width = 0.82) +
  geom_col(aes(y = range1), fill = "grey55", width = 0.82) +
  geom_col(aes(y = current), fill = "black", width = 0.32) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(y = target, ymin = target, ymax = target),
    colour = "red",
    width = 0.38,
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Bullet Chart of Product Sales",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Sales"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Observation: The black bars and red target markers make the performance comparison very direct.

Insight: A bullet chart is a good dashboard choice because it is compact and allows many products to be compared in one panel.

4 Plotting sparklines using ggplot2

4.1 Preparing sparkline support data

Show code 
sales_report <- report_base %>%
  select(Month, Product, Sales)

mins <- sales_report %>%
  group_by(Product) %>%
  slice_min(order_by = Sales, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup()

maxs <- sales_report %>%
  group_by(Product) %>%
  slice_max(order_by = Sales, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup()

ends <- sales_report %>%
  group_by(Product) %>%
  filter(Month == max(Month)) %>%
  ungroup()

quarts <- sales_report %>%
  group_by(Product) %>%
  summarise(
    quart1 = quantile(Sales, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    quart2 = quantile(Sales, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  right_join(sales_report, by = "Product")

4.2 Building the ggplot sparkline panel

Show code 
ggplot(sales_report, aes(x = Month, y = Sales)) +
  facet_grid(Product ~ ., scales = "free_y") +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = quarts,
    aes(ymin = quart1, ymax = quart2),
    fill = "grey92"
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.35, colour = "grey35") +
  geom_point(data = mins, colour = "red", size = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = maxs, colour = "blue", size = 0.9) +
  geom_text(data = mins, aes(label = Sales), vjust = -1, size = 2) +
  geom_text(data = maxs, aes(label = Sales), vjust = 2.5, size = 2) +
  geom_text(data = ends, aes(label = Sales), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.45, size = 2) +
  geom_text(data = ends, aes(label = Product), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 1.0, size = 2.2) +
  expand_limits(x = max(sales_report$Month) + 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0.1, 0)) +
  ggthemes::theme_tufte(base_size = 7, base_family = "sans") +
  theme(
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_blank()
  )

Observation: The sparkline panel shows each product’s monthly movement in a very small space.

Insight: This design is useful when the dashboard needs to emphasise trend instead of only one final total.

5.1 Creating the list-column for monthly sales

Show code 
report <- report_base %>%

5.2 A simple bullet chart table

Show code 
if (has_gtextras) {
  product %>%
    gt() %>%
    gt_plt_bullet(
      column = current,
      target = target,
      width = 60,
      palette = c("lightblue", "black")
    ) %>%
    gt_theme_538()
} else {
  product %>%
    gt() %>%
    fmt_number(columns = c(current, target), decimals = 0)

  summarise(

6 Interactive information dashboard design: reactable methods

The original chapter uses reactablefmtr, but that package is not always easy to install on every R version. To keep this file stable and still preserve hover values, I create the interactive section with reactable and custom HTML mini charts.

6.1 Helper functions for custom hover charts

Show code 
make_sparkbar <- function(values, labels = month.abb[seq_along(values)]) {
  values <- as.numeric(values)
  vmax <- max(values, na.rm = TRUE)
  vmean <- mean(values, na.rm = TRUE)
  min_id <- which.min(values)[1]
  max_id <- which.max(values)[1]

  mean_y <- if (vmax == 0) 0 else round(vmean / vmax * 26, 1)

  bars <- lapply(seq_along(values), function(i) {
    fill_col <- if (i == min_id) {
      "#d62728"
    } else if (i == max_id) {
      "#1f77b4"
    } else {
      "#9aa5b1"
    }

    bar_height <- if (vmax == 0) 2 else max(2, round(values[i] / vmax * 26))

    htmltools::tags$div(
      title = paste0(labels[i], ": ", scales::comma(values[i])),
      style = paste0(
        "flex:1; height:", bar_height,
        "px; background:", fill_col,
        "; border-radius:1px;"
      )
    )
  })

  htmltools::tags$div(
    style = "position:relative; width:230px; height:34px; padding-top:4px;",
    htmltools::tags$div(
      style = paste0(
        "position:absolute; left:0; right:0; bottom:",
        3 + mean_y,
        "px; border-top:1px dashed #d62728; opacity:0.9;"
      )
    ),
    htmltools::tags$div(
      style = "position:absolute; left:0; right:0; bottom:3px; display:flex; align-items:flex-end; gap:2px; height:26px;",
      htmltools::tagList(bars)
    ),
    htmltools::tags$div(
      style = "position:absolute; left:0; right:0; bottom:0; border-top:1px solid #d8d8d8;"
    )
  )
}

make_sparkline <- function(values, labels = month.abb[seq_along(values)]) {
  values <- as.numeric(values)
  n <- length(values)
  width <- 230
  height <- 42
  pad <- 7

  minv <- min(values, na.rm = TRUE)
  maxv <- max(values, na.rm = TRUE)
  rng <- maxv - minv
  if (rng == 0) rng <- 1

  xs <- seq(pad, width - pad, length.out = n)
  ys <- height - pad - ((values - minv) / rng) * (height - 2 * pad)
  mean_y <- height - pad - ((mean(values, na.rm = TRUE) - minv) / rng) * (height - 2 * pad)

  point_string <- paste(sprintf("%.1f,%.1f", xs, ys), collapse = " ")

  circle_string <- paste(
    vapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
      fill_col <- if (i == which.min(values)[1]) {
        "#d62728"
      } else if (i == which.max(values)[1] || i == n) {
        "#1f77b4"
      } else {
        "#000000"
      }

      opacity_val <- if (i %in% c(which.min(values)[1], which.max(values)[1], n)) {
        "0.95"
      } else {
        "0.001"
      }

      paste0(
        '<circle cx="', round(xs[i], 1),
        '" cy="', round(ys[i], 1),
        '" r="3.2" fill="', fill_col,
        '" fill-opacity="', opacity_val,
        '"><title>', labels[i], ': ', scales::comma(values[i]), '</title></circle>'
      )
    }, character(1)),
    collapse = ""
  )

  svg_txt <- paste0(
    '<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="', width,
    '" height="', height,
    '" viewBox="0 0 ', width, ' ', height, '">',
    '<line x1="', pad, '" x2="', width - pad,
    '" y1="', round(mean_y, 1), '" y2="', round(mean_y, 1),
    '" stroke="#d62728" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/>',
    '<polyline fill="none" stroke="#6b7f99" stroke-width="1.3" points="', point_string, '"/>',
    circle_string,
    '<text x="0" y="13" font-size="10" fill="#444">', scales::comma(values[1]), '</text>',
    '<text x="', width - 30, '" y="13" font-size="10" fill="#444">', scales::comma(values[n]), '</text>',
    '</svg>'
  )

  htmltools::HTML(svg_txt)
}

6.2 Preparing the interactive report table

Show code 
report_interactive <- report_base %>%
  group_by(Product) %>%
  summarise(
    `Monthly Sales` = list(Sales),
    Average = mean(Sales, na.rm = TRUE),
    Total = sum(Sales, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

6.3 Interactive sparkbar table with hover values

Show code 
reactable(
  report_interactive,
  defaultPageSize = 13,
  compact = TRUE,
  striped = TRUE,
  highlight = TRUE,
  searchable = FALSE,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(minWidth = 170),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      html = TRUE,
      minWidth = 250,
      cell = function(value) make_sparkbar(unlist(value))
    ),
    Average = colDef(format = colFormat(separators = TRUE, digits = 1)),
    Total = colDef(format = colFormat(separators = TRUE, digits = 0))
  )
)

Observation: This view is close to a dashboard strip chart, and the monthly values can be seen by moving the mouse over each small bar.

Insight: This approach is more stable than depending on extra GitHub-only packages, so it is practical for assignment rendering.

6.4 Interactive sparkline table with hover values

Show code 
reactable(
  report_interactive,
  defaultPageSize = 13,
  compact = TRUE,
  striped = TRUE,
  highlight = TRUE,
  searchable = FALSE,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(minWidth = 170),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      name = "Sales Trend",
      html = TRUE,
      minWidth = 250,
      cell = function(value) make_sparkline(unlist(value))
    ),
    Average = colDef(format = colFormat(separators = TRUE, digits = 1)),
    Total = colDef(format = colFormat(separators = TRUE, digits = 0))
  )
)

Observation: The sparkline version is better for reading the shape of the trend, while the red dashed line adds a useful reference for the mean level.

Insight: Compared with the sparkbar view, this design is more suitable when the user wants to focus on fluctuations over time.

7 Conclusion

This exercise shows that dashboard design is not only about producing one attractive chart. A better dashboard usually combines compact comparisons, trend summaries, and table layout in the same page.

From this practice, I found that ggplot2 is useful for building chart logic clearly, gt and gtExtras are useful for static dashboard tables, and reactable is helpful for creating lightweight interactive dashboard views. In my final version, I used a stable custom reactable solution so the file can render more smoothly while still keeping hover values.

8 Reference

  • R for Visual Analytics, Chapter 31: Information Dashboard Design: R methods.

This hands-on exercise is based on Chapter 31, which focuses on information dashboard design in R. In this page, I work on three main ideas: bullet charts, sparklines, and dashboard-style tables.

## Getting started

required_pkgs <- c(

if (length(missing_required) > 0) {

    install.packages(missing_optional, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org"),

## Bullet chart in ggplot2

The chart below recreates the product-level bullet chart idea from the chapter. The grey bars provide reference ranges, the black bar shows actual sales, and the red marker shows the target value.

```{r}
bullet_data <- product %>%
  mutate(
    range3 = pmax(target, current) * 1.05,
    range2 = target * 0.80,
    range1 = target * 0.50

ggplot(bullet_data, aes(x = Product)) +
  geom_col(aes(y = range3), fill = "grey85", width = 0.82) +
  geom_col(aes(y = range2), fill = "grey70", width = 0.82) +
  geom_col(aes(y = range1), fill = "grey55", width = 0.82) +
  geom_col(aes(y = current), fill = "black", width = 0.32) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(y = target, ymin = target, ymax = target),
    colour = "red",
    width = 0.38,
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Bullet Chart of Product Sales",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Sales"

```

Observation: The black bars and red target markers make the performance comparison very direct.

Insight: A bullet chart is a good dashboard choice because it is compact and allows many products to be compared in one panel.

```{r}
ggplot(sales_report, aes(x = Month, y = Sales)) +
  facet_grid(Product ~ ., scales = "free_y") +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = quarts,
    aes(ymin = quart1, ymax = quart2),
    fill = "grey92"
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.35, colour = "grey35") +
  geom_point(data = mins, colour = "red", size = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = maxs, colour = "blue", size = 0.9) +
  geom_text(data = mins, aes(label = Sales), vjust = -1, size = 2) +
  geom_text(data = maxs, aes(label = Sales), vjust = 2.5, size = 2) +
  geom_text(data = ends, aes(label = Sales), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.45, size = 2) +
  geom_text(data = ends, aes(label = Product), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 1.0, size = 2.2) +
  expand_limits(x = max(sales_report$Month) + 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0.1, 0)) +
  ggthemes::theme_tufte(base_size = 7, base_family = "sans") +
  theme(
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_blank()
  )
```

Observation: The sparkline panel shows each product's monthly movement in a very small space.

Insight: This design is useful when the dashboard needs to emphasise trend instead of only one final total.

## Static information dashboard design: gt and gtExtras methods

### Creating the list-column for monthly sales

```{r}
report <- report_base %>%
  group_by(Product) %>%
  summarise(
    `Monthly Sales` = list(Sales),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

### A simple bullet chart table

```{r}
if (has_gtextras) {
  product %>%
    gt() %>%
    gt_plt_bullet(
      column = current,
      target = target,
      width = 60,
      palette = c("lightblue", "black")
    ) %>%
    gt_theme_538()
} else {
  product %>%
    gt() %>%
    fmt_number(columns = c(current, target), decimals = 0)
}
```

Observation: Embedding the bullet chart inside a table makes the output look more like a real dashboard.

Insight: This format is useful for management reporting because the chart and labels stay together in one place.

### Basic sparkline table

```{r}
if (has_gtextras) {
  report %>%
    gt() %>%
    gt_plt_sparkline(`Monthly Sales`, same_limit = FALSE)
} else {
  report %>%
    mutate(`Monthly Sales` = purrr::map_chr(`Monthly Sales`, ~ paste(.x, collapse = ", "))) %>%
    gt()
}
```

### Adding summary statistics

```{r}
sales <- report_base %>%
  group_by(Product) %>%
  summarise(
    Min = min(Sales, na.rm = TRUE),
    Max = max(Sales, na.rm = TRUE),
    Average = mean(Sales, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

sales %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(columns = Average, decimals = 2)
```

### Combining statistics and sparklines

```{r}
sales_data <- left_join(sales, report, by = "Product")

if (has_gtextras) {
  sales_data %>%
    gt() %>%
    gt_plt_sparkline(`Monthly Sales`, same_limit = FALSE) %>%
    fmt_number(columns = Average, decimals = 2)
} else {
  sales_data %>%
    mutate(`Monthly Sales` = purrr::map_chr(`Monthly Sales`, ~ paste(.x, collapse = ", "))) %>%
    gt() %>%
    fmt_number(columns = Average, decimals = 2)
}
```

### Combining sparklines and bullet charts

```{r}
bullet <- report_base %>%
  group_by(Product) %>%
  summarise(
    Target = sum(`Budget Sales`, na.rm = TRUE),
    Actual = sum(Sales, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

sales_data2 <- left_join(sales_data, bullet, by = "Product")

if (has_gtextras) {
  sales_data2 %>%
    gt() %>%
    gt_plt_sparkline(`Monthly Sales`) %>%
    gt_plt_bullet(
      column = Actual,
      target = Target,
      width = 28,
      palette = c("lightblue", "black")
    ) %>%
    fmt_number(columns = Average, decimals = 2) %>%
    gt_theme_538()
} else {
  sales_data2 %>%
    mutate(`Monthly Sales` = purrr::map_chr(`Monthly Sales`, ~ paste(.x, collapse = ", "))) %>%
    gt() %>%
    fmt_number(columns = Average, decimals = 2)
}
```

Observation: This combined table is much closer to a practical dashboard because it brings trend, level, and target information together.

Insight: A compact dashboard often works best when multiple small views are placed in one aligned table.

## Interactive information dashboard design: reactable methods

The original chapter uses `reactablefmtr`, but that package is not always easy to install on every R version. To keep this file stable and still preserve hover values, I create the interactive section with `reactable` and custom HTML mini charts.

### Helper functions for custom hover charts

```{r}
make_sparkbar <- function(values, labels = month.abb[seq_along(values)]) {
  values <- as.numeric(values)
  vmax <- max(values, na.rm = TRUE)
  vmean <- mean(values, na.rm = TRUE)
  min_id <- which.min(values)[1]
  max_id <- which.max(values)[1]

  mean_y <- if (vmax == 0) 0 else round(vmean / vmax * 26, 1)

  bars <- lapply(seq_along(values), function(i) {
    fill_col <- if (i == min_id) {
      "#d62728"
    } else if (i == max_id) {
      "#1f77b4"
    } else {
      "#9aa5b1"
    }

    bar_height <- if (vmax == 0) 2 else max(2, round(values[i] / vmax * 26))

    htmltools::tags$div(
      title = paste0(labels[i], ": ", scales::comma(values[i])),
      style = paste0(
        "flex:1; height:", bar_height,
        "px; background:", fill_col,
        "; border-radius:1px;"
      )
    )
  })

  htmltools::tags$div(
    style = "position:relative; width:230px; height:34px; padding-top:4px;",
    htmltools::tags$div(
      style = paste0(
        "position:absolute; left:0; right:0; bottom:",
        3 + mean_y,
        "px; border-top:1px dashed #d62728; opacity:0.9;"
      )
    ),
    htmltools::tags$div(
      style = "position:absolute; left:0; right:0; bottom:3px; display:flex; align-items:flex-end; gap:2px; height:26px;",
      htmltools::tagList(bars)
    ),
    htmltools::tags$div(
      style = "position:absolute; left:0; right:0; bottom:0; border-top:1px solid #d8d8d8;"
    )
  )
}

make_sparkline <- function(values, labels = month.abb[seq_along(values)]) {
  values <- as.numeric(values)
  n <- length(values)
  width <- 230
  height <- 42
  pad <- 7

  minv <- min(values, na.rm = TRUE)
  maxv <- max(values, na.rm = TRUE)
  rng <- maxv - minv
  if (rng == 0) rng <- 1

  xs <- seq(pad, width - pad, length.out = n)
  ys <- height - pad - ((values - minv) / rng) * (height - 2 * pad)
  mean_y <- height - pad - ((mean(values, na.rm = TRUE) - minv) / rng) * (height - 2 * pad)

  point_string <- paste(sprintf("%.1f,%.1f", xs, ys), collapse = " ")

  circle_string <- paste(
    vapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
      fill_col <- if (i == which.min(values)[1]) {
        "#d62728"
      } else if (i == which.max(values)[1] || i == n) {
        "#1f77b4"
      } else {
        "#000000"
      }

      opacity_val <- if (i %in% c(which.min(values)[1], which.max(values)[1], n)) {
        "0.95"
      } else {
        "0.001"
      }

      paste0(
        '<circle cx="', round(xs[i], 1),
        '" cy="', round(ys[i], 1),
        '" r="3.2" fill="', fill_col,
        '" fill-opacity="', opacity_val,
        '"><title>', labels[i], ': ', scales::comma(values[i]), '</title></circle>'
      )
    }, character(1)),
    collapse = ""
  )

  svg_txt <- paste0(
    '<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="', width,
    '" height="', height,
    '" viewBox="0 0 ', width, ' ', height, '">',
    '<line x1="', pad, '" x2="', width - pad,
    '" y1="', round(mean_y, 1), '" y2="', round(mean_y, 1),
    '" stroke="#d62728" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/>',
    '<polyline fill="none" stroke="#6b7f99" stroke-width="1.3" points="', point_string, '"/>',
    circle_string,
    '<text x="0" y="13" font-size="10" fill="#444">', scales::comma(values[1]), '</text>',
    '<text x="', width - 30, '" y="13" font-size="10" fill="#444">', scales::comma(values[n]), '</text>',
    '</svg>'
  )

  htmltools::HTML(svg_txt)
}
```

### Preparing the interactive report table

```{r}
report_interactive <- report_base %>%
  group_by(Product) %>%
  summarise(
    `Monthly Sales` = list(Sales),
    Average = mean(Sales, na.rm = TRUE),
    Total = sum(Sales, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

### Interactive sparkbar table with hover values

```{r}
reactable(
  report_interactive,
  defaultPageSize = 13,
  compact = TRUE,
  striped = TRUE,
  highlight = TRUE,
  searchable = FALSE,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(minWidth = 170),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      html = TRUE,
      minWidth = 250,
      cell = function(value) make_sparkbar(unlist(value))
    ),
    Average = colDef(format = colFormat(separators = TRUE, digits = 1)),
    Total = colDef(format = colFormat(separators = TRUE, digits = 0))
  )
)
```

Observation: This view is close to a dashboard strip chart, and the monthly values can be seen by moving the mouse over each small bar.

Insight: This approach is more stable than depending on extra GitHub-only packages, so it is practical for assignment rendering.

### Interactive sparkline table with hover values

```{r}
reactable(
  report_interactive,
  defaultPageSize = 13,
  compact = TRUE,
  striped = TRUE,
  highlight = TRUE,
  searchable = FALSE,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(minWidth = 170),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      name = "Sales Trend",
      html = TRUE,
      minWidth = 250,
      cell = function(value) make_sparkline(unlist(value))
    ),
    Average = colDef(format = colFormat(separators = TRUE, digits = 1)),
    Total = colDef(format = colFormat(separators = TRUE, digits = 0))
  )
)
```

Observation: The sparkline version is better for reading the shape of the trend, while the red dashed line adds a useful reference for the mean level.

Insight: Compared with the sparkbar view, this design is more suitable when the user wants to focus on fluctuations over time.

## Conclusion

This exercise shows that dashboard design is not only about producing one attractive chart. A better dashboard usually combines compact comparisons, trend summaries, and table layout in the same page.

From this practice, I found that `ggplot2` is useful for building chart logic clearly, `gt` and `gtExtras` are useful for static dashboard tables, and `reactable` is helpful for creating lightweight interactive dashboard views. In my final version, I used a stable custom `reactable` solution so the file can render more smoothly while still keeping hover values.
